breakfast.name: Tamagoyaki (Rolled Omelet)
breakfast.description: A sweet and savory rolled omelet, traditional Japanese breakfast dish served with rice and miso soup
instructions: Beat eggs in a bowl
Mix in mirin, soy sauce, and salt
Heat a rectangular tamago pan over medium heat and lightly oil it
Pour 1/4 of egg mixture into pan, tilting to spread evenly
When set but still slightly moist, roll from one end using chopsticks
Push rolled egg to far end of pan
Oil empty space, pour 1/3 of remaining egg mixture
Roll again, incorporating first roll
Repeat process until all egg is used
Transfer to cutting board and slice
Serve warm with rice
breakfast.notes: The key is rolling while the outer layer is set but center is still wet. A rectangular pan (tamagoyaki pan) makes it easier
breakfast.fun_fact: Tamagoyaki is a staple of bento boxes and Japanese school lunches. The technique of rolling teaches patience and precision, values central to Japanese cooking
alternatives: Regular non-stick pan instead of tamago pan
Add dashi or kombu tea to the egg mixture for deeper umami
Serve with tonkatsu sauce instead of plain

breakfast.name: Onigiri (Rice Balls)
breakfast.description: Hand-formed rice balls with various fillings, a popular Japanese breakfast and snack food
instructions: Cool cooked rice slightly
Wet your hands with water and sprinkle salt on palm
Place about 3/4 cup rice in center of your hand
Make indent with thumb in center of rice
Add 1 tsp umeboshi paste or bonito flakes
Cover filling with more rice
Gently form into triangle or ball shape
Wrap a strip of nori seaweed around base
Sprinkle sesame seeds on top
Arrange on plate with nori seaweed
breakfast.notes: Keep hands wet throughout the process to prevent rice from sticking. The filling should be in the very center
breakfast.fun_fact: Onigiri appears in countless manga and anime, representing comfort and home-cooked meals in Japanese culture
alternatives: Grilled salmon instead of bonito
Canned tuna mixed with mayo
Kelp (kombu) instead of umeboshi
Round shape instead of triangular

lunch.name: Maki Sushi (Sushi Rolls)
lunch.description: Seasoned rice rolled with vegetables and/or fish, sliced into rounds. Requires practice but fundamental to Japanese cuisine
ingredients: 6 oz sashimi-grade fish or imitation crab
instructions: Mix rice vinegar, sugar, and salt
Toss with warm sushi rice until rice cools
Place nori shiny side down on bamboo mat
Spread thin layer of sushi rice on nori, leaving 1 inch at top
Arrange filling ingredients in line across middle of rice
Use mat to roll nori tightly, sealing edge with water
Let sit 5 minutes, then slice with wet knife into 6-8 pieces
Serve with soy sauce, wasabi, and pickled ginger
lunch.notes: Sashimi-grade fish must be used. A bamboo mat (makisu) is essential. Wet your knife between cuts
lunch.fun_fact: Maki sushi as we know it is a relatively recent innovation from the Edo period, created when soy sauce became affordable enough for common people to use
alternatives: Vegetable-only rolls for vegetarians
Inside-out rolls (uramaki) with rice on outside
Different fish: tuna, salmon, or scallop
Cooked ingredients instead of raw

lunch.name: Ramen (Noodle Soup)
lunch.description: Rich broth with wheat noodles and toppings. The broth requires hours of simmering for authentic depth
ingredients: 2 lbs chicken bones or pork bones
instructions: Blanch bones in boiling water for 2 minutes, rinse
In 8-quart pot, combine bones with 8 cups water
Add kombu and bring to boil, then simmer 30 minutes
Remove kombu, add bonito flakes and simmer 10 more minutes
Strain, discard solids
In separate pan, sauté garlic and ginger in oil
Add broth back, add soy sauce, mirin, and salt
Simmer 30 minutes more to develop flavor
Cook ramen noodles according to package
Divide noodles into bowls
Pour broth over noodles
Top with egg halves, chashu, bean sprouts, scallions, and nori
lunch.notes: Authentic ramen broth requires hours to develop. Many Japanese home cooks use a pressure cooker to speed up the process
lunch.fun_fact: Instant ramen was invented in Japan in 1958 and has become a global phenomenon. Traditional ramen shops are regarded with reverence in Japanese food culture
alternatives: Chicken broth for lighter tonkotsu
Vegetable broth for vegetarian version
Pre-made ramen broth to save time
Different toppings: corn, bamboo shoots, seaweed

dinner.name: Tempura (Battered and Fried)
dinner.description: Vegetables and seafood coated in delicate batter and deep-fried until crispy. Served with dipping sauce
ingredients: 2 cups vegetables (eggplant, bell pepper, mushrooms, sweet potato)
instructions: Mix dashi, soy sauce, and mirin to create dipping sauce
Combine flour, cornstarch, and salt
Beat egg yolks with ice water
Gently fold wet ingredients into dry (batter should be lumpy)
Heat oil to 350°F
Pat vegetables and seafood dry
Dip pieces into batter, coating lightly
Deep fry in batches 2-3 minutes until golden
Drain on paper towels
Serve immediately with dipping sauce and daikon-ginger mixture
Let sauce cool slightly before dipping
dinner.notes: Ice-cold water and cold batter are key to crispy texture. Do not overmix the batter—lumps are desired
dinner.fun_fact: Tempura was introduced to Japan by Portuguese traders in the 16th century. The word comes from 'tempero' (Portuguese seasoning)
alternatives: Store-bought tempura mix for quick version
Different vegetables based on season
Shrimp only or fish only
Serve with ponzu instead of dashi sauce

dinner.name: Tonkatsu (Breaded Pork Cutlet)
dinner.description: Pork loin breaded and deep-fried until crispy. Served with tonkatsu sauce, cabbage slaw, and rice
instructions: Pound pork cutlets to 1/4 inch thickness
Season with salt and pepper
Set up breading station: flour, beaten egg, panko
Coat pork in flour, shaking off excess
Dip in egg, then coat completely in panko
Press panko gently so it adheres
Heat oil to 350°F
Fry cutlets 3-4 minutes per side until golden brown
Drain on paper towels
Mix tonkatsu sauce with Worcestershire
Serve with cabbage slaw and sauce drizzled on top
dinner.notes: Panko creates a crispier, lighter crust than regular breadcrumbs. Pound evenly to ensure even cooking
dinner.fun_fact: Tonkatsu is a Western-influenced dish that became uniquely Japanese. It's often served in Japanese 'katsu' specialty restaurants
alternatives: Chicken instead of pork
Mushroom or eggplant for vegetarian version
Serve with curry sauce instead of tonkatsu sauce
Oven-baked instead of deep-fried for lighter option

snacks.name: Takoyaki (Octopus Balls)
snacks.description: Golf ball-sized battered octopus pieces, deep-fried and served with takoyaki sauce, bonito flakes, and aonori
instructions: Mix flour, baking powder, and salt
Whisk egg with dashi
Combine wet and dry ingredients until smooth batter forms
Heat takoyaki pan (specialized pan with half-round molds) over medium-high heat
Oil each mold lightly
Pour batter into molds, filling halfway
Add piece of octopus, pinch of scallion
Fill rest with batter
Use picks to rotate takoyaki as edges cook (turning constantly)
Cook 8-10 minutes until golden brown all over
Transfer to plate
Drizzle with takoyaki sauce and mayo
Top with bonito flakes and aonori
Serve immediately while hot
snacks.notes: A takoyaki pan is essential for authentic shape. Rotating constantly ensures even cooking and spherical shape
snacks.fun_fact: Takoyaki originated in Osaka in 1935 and is now one of Japan's most beloved street foods. The bonito flakes dance from the heat of the takoyaki
alternatives: Cooked shrimp instead of octopus
Cheese and mozzarella for variation
Okonomiyaki flour mix instead of making batter from scratch
Make in muffin tins in oven for easier preparation

desserts.name: Mochi (Rice Cake)
desserts.description: Chewy glutinous rice cake, often filled with red bean paste or ice cream
instructions: Mix glutinous rice flour, sugar, and salt
Gradually add water, stirring until smooth dough forms
Microwave in microwave-safe bowl for 2 minutes on high
Stir well, microwave 1 more minute
Cool slightly until handle-able
Dust work surface with cornstarch
Divide dough into 12 pieces
Flatten each piece into thin circle
Place 1 tbsp red bean paste in center
Fold edges up and seal, then gently round shape
Dust with cornstarch to prevent sticking
Serve at room temperature or slightly chilled
desserts.notes: The dough must be handled quickly after cooking as it hardens as it cools. Work in batches if needed
desserts.fun_fact: Mochi is eaten year-round but particularly on New Year's Day in Japan for good luck. Freshly made mochi is a delicacy
alternatives: Mochi ice cream as filling
Different bean paste flavors (black bean, adzuki)
Sesame paste filling
Store-bought mochi wrappers to save time

drinks.name: Matcha Tea (Ceremonial Powdered Green Tea)
drinks.description: Bright green powdered tea whisked with hot water. Central to Japanese tea ceremony
instructions: Heat water to 160-180°F (not boiling)
Sift matcha powder into ceramic bowl to prevent lumps
Add small amount of hot water (1-2 tbsp)
Use bamboo whisk to make a paste, breaking up any lumps
Add remaining hot water
Whisk vigorously in M-shaped motion until frothy
Whisk should create foam on surface
Drink immediately while foam is still present
drinks.notes: Temperature is critical—boiling water will make the tea bitter. Use ceremonial-grade matcha for best results
drinks.fun_fact: Matcha is used in the Japanese tea ceremony, a mindful practice emphasizing harmony, respect, and tranquility
alternatives: Culinary-grade matcha for everyday drinking
Mix with milk for matcha latte
Add honey or sugar if too bitter
Blend with ice for iced matcha

drinks.name: Sake (Japanese Rice Wine)
drinks.description: Traditional Japanese rice wine with complex flavors. Requires specialized fermentation and is typically purchased from breweries
instructions: This is a complex fermentation process typically done by professional breweries
Serve chilled in small ceramic cups or warmed in traditional sake bottles
Pour small amounts to share with others
Taste slowly and mindfully
drinks.notes: Premium sake (ginjo) uses more polished rice. Lower-grade sake (futsushu) uses less polished rice
drinks.fun_fact: Sake is often called 'nihonshu' (Japanese alcohol). It has been brewed for over 2000 years and is central to Japanese culture and Shinto rituals
alternatives: Buy different grades and styles from local sake breweries
Plum wine (umeshu) for sweeter alternative
Shochu for stronger spirit
